newsitem.title: UK: Japan baulks at yen fall but further weakness seen.
newsitem.headline: Japan baulks at yen fall but further weakness seen.

text.p: Japanese officials are dishing out plenty of verbal intervention in an attempt to stem the yen's decline, after it hit a 45-month low of 117.00 per dollar on Monday, but analysts see further weakness at least in the near-term.
"An excessively weak or strong yen is not favourable for the Japanese economy," finance minister Hiroshi Mitsuzuka said on Tuesday. "We want exchange rates to stabilise."
This followed similar comments by vice finance minister Tadashi Ogawa on Monday who also said Japan would act to prevent excessive movements in forex rates.

Analysts said with the Nikkei stock index falling nearly three percent below the key psychological 19,000 level on Tuesday, the outlook for the yen in the near-term is not bright, but further out the picture of sustained weakness is not a clear one.

"Stock market nerves feed through into the currency, which in turn increases the attractiveness of overseas assets, weakens the domestic market and further pressures the currency," said Nick Parsons, currency strategist at Banque Paribas. "We have a bit of a vicious circle in Japan at the moment."

Analysts said overseas investors were aggressive buyers of the Japanese stock market up until the summer of last year with British funds tending to be underweight of the U.S. market and overweight Japan.
But foreigners have been net sellers of the Nikkei since the summer and stocks have come down.

"Officials are clearly concerned that further weakening of the yen will limit overseas investor interest in the market," said Tim Fox, treasury economist at Standard Chartered. "This is one of the reasons for trying to talk some stability into the currency."
There is also a problem regards domestic portfolio flows and that could be crucial for the yen.

"The key to where the yen goes is what the Japanese do with their money," said Gerard Lyons, chief economist at DKB International. "Given weak growth and low yields at home Japanese investors have to put more money overseas. At the moment it's a trickle but it will get larger and push the yen weaker."
However, actual intervention is possible to stop the yen's fall and with Japanese reserves at a record level for the 34th consecutive month, the Bank of Japan has plenty of ammunition.
From early 1994 and into 1996 the Bank of Japan aggressively bought dollars in an attempt to push it higher to bail out Japanese exporters who were seeing export markets dry-up due to the strong yen.
Also, while most of the talk is centred around dollar/yen and the U.S. attitude to the yen's decline analysts said a key factor will be the European attitude.
It is hard to see continental Europe standing idly by and hand Japan a massive competitive advantage.

Mark/yen's four year average is 66.00 and it is currently trading around 74.00, noted Paribas' Parsons. "Mark/yen is still more than 10 percent above its long-term average which is effectively providing a subsidy to Japanese exporters at the expense of German.
"Waigel (German finance minister Theo) has already said EMU and its impact on currency markets will be on the agenda at the G7 meeting on February 8 in Berlin," Parsons said.
"We think the discussion will be broadened out to include the yen and we don't think they will be willing to accept further yen weakness from here."

On top of this it is getting close to the time of year when Japanese investors will start to realise profits on overseas investments for fiscal end-year book closings, Kenneth Landon, currency analyst at Deutsche Morgan Grenfell.

"Since 1993 dollar/yen has fallen in each February as fiscal end-year funds repatriation exerted a strong influence. Last year, these funds flows were strong enough to impel the Bank of Japan to buy a monthly record $17 billion support dollar/yen, he said.
